lead: Liquid–liquid extraction removes a solute from a liquid feed by mixing the feed with a second liquid, the solvent, that dissolves the solute but hardly mixes with the feed liquid. After mixing, the liquids settle into two layers that share the solute. Extraction is chosen when distillation is poor: close boiling points, a little high-boiling solute in much water (dilute acetic acid), or a heat-sensitive solute (penicillin). Because three components are present, the compositions are read from a triangular (ternary) diagram.

sections.h3: Names of the streams and what makes a good solvent

blocks.text: Call the solute A, the feed liquid that carries it B (the carrier or diluent) and the added liquid S (the solvent). The solvent-rich layer that leaves is the extract (E); the carrier-rich layer is the raffinate (R). A stage is one mixing followed by one settling. In an ideal (equilibrium) stage the extract and raffinate leave in equilibrium with each other. The solvent is later distilled off the extract and reused.
Syllabi list the solvent characteristics below. Each one has a reason you should be able to state in the exam.

items: Selectivity β = (yA/yB)/(xA/xB), where y is a mass fraction in the extract and x in the raffinate. β must be well above 1, or the extract carries as much carrier as solute and nothing is separated.
Distribution coefficient K = yA/xA large, so little solvent is needed.
Low mutual solubility of B and S: less solvent lost in the raffinate and a purer extract.
Recoverability: a boiling point well away from that of A and no azeotrope with it, so the solvent can be distilled off and recycled.
Density difference between the layers large enough to settle quickly; interfacial tension high enough for drops to coalesce but not so high that the liquids cannot be dispersed.
Low viscosity, stability, low toxicity and flammability, low cost.

blocks.text: The three mass fractions add to 1, so a mixture is fixed by two numbers and fits on a triangle. Each corner is a pure component: A at the top, B at the bottom left, S at the bottom right. A point on a side is a two-component mixture. For a point inside, the fraction of A is its perpendicular distance from the side BS divided by the height of the triangle; the same rule with the other two sides gives B and S. In practice you read the grid lines drawn parallel to the sides.

The binodal (solubility) curve divides the diagram. Mixtures outside it form one liquid phase. A mixture inside it splits into two layers whose compositions lie on the curve: the raffinate branch near B and the extract branch near S. The straight line joining two layers in equilibrium is a tie line; tie lines are measured, and the overall mixture point always lies on its tie line. Tie lines usually slope, because the solute is not equally distributed. They get shorter as the solute content rises and shrink to a single point, the plait point, where the two layers become identical. Beyond it no separation is possible.

Type I systems have one partly miscible pair (B–S) and a plait point; water–acetic acid–isopropyl ether is the usual textbook case. Type II systems have two partly miscible pairs (A–S and B–S), so the two-phase band runs right across the diagram with no plait point.

Lever rule. When F kg of feed and S kg of solvent are mixed, the mixture point M lies on the straight line FS, with FM/MS = S/F. When M splits into E and R on a tie line, E/M = RM/RE and R/M = ME/RE. The lever rule is a mass balance drawn as a picture, so it can always be checked with the component balances.
K = y<sub>A</sub> / x<sub>A</sub>      Y = y<sub>A</sub>/(1 − y<sub>A</sub>),  X = x<sub>A</sub>/(1 − x<sub>A</sub>)
blocks.where: K is the distribution coefficient on mass fractions at the two ends of one tie line. X is kg A per kg of the rest of the raffinate (nearly all B) and Y is kg A per kg of the rest of the extract (nearly all S). The ratio form is used when B and S are almost immiscible, because then the B flow and the S flow stay constant from stage to stage.

blocks.text: K changes along the binodal curve and with temperature, so one K is used only over a range where it is nearly constant. When B and S are almost immiscible the stage calculations become simple algebra on X and Y; that is the route of the next two chapters. When they are partly miscible, the stages are drawn on the triangle.

examples.question: 100 kg of a feed containing 30 mass% acetic acid (A) in water (B) is mixed in one ideal stage with 120 kg of pure solvent S. The tie line through the mixture point joins a raffinate of x<sub>A</sub> = 0.100, x<sub>S</sub> = 0.030, x<sub>B</sub> = 0.870 to an extract of y<sub>A</sub> = 0.1543, y<sub>S</sub> = 0.800, y<sub>B</sub> = 0.0457. Find the mixture point, the masses of extract and raffinate, the acid recovered, K and the selectivity.
steps: Mixture: M = F + S = 100 + 120 = 220 kg. It holds 30 kg A, 70 kg B and 120 kg S, so x<sub>A,M</sub> = 30/220 = 0.1364, x<sub>S,M</sub> = 120/220 = 0.5455, x<sub>B,M</sub> = 70/220 = 0.3182. Lever check on line FS: FM/MS = 120/100 = 1.2.

Check the other components. Solvent: 0.800 × 147.3 + 0.030 × 72.7 = 117.9 + 2.2 = 120.1 kg (fed 120). Water: 0.0457 × 147.3 + 0.870 × 72.7 = 6.7 + 63.2 = 69.9 kg (fed 70). The small differences are rounding of the tie-line ends.
Lever rule: E/M = RM/RE = 0.669, so E = 0.669 × 220 = 147.3 kg, the same answer read as lengths on the diagram.
Acid in extract = 0.1543 × 147.3 = 22.7 kg, so 22.7/30 = 75.8 % of the acid is recovered in one stage. Acid left in raffinate = 0.100 × 72.7 = 7.3 kg.
K = 0.1543/0.100 = 1.54. Selectivity β = (0.1543/0.0457)/(0.100/0.870) = 3.38/0.115 = 29.4, far above 1, so the solvent takes acid much more readily than water.
examples.answer: M lies at x<sub>A</sub> = 0.136, x<sub>S</sub> = 0.545; E = 147.3 kg, R = 72.7 kg; 22.7 kg acid (75.8 %) goes to the extract; K = 1.54 and β = 29.4.

traps: Tie lines are measured lines through the two equilibrium layers. A line drawn parallel to a side of the triangle is a line of constant composition of one component, not a tie line.
The mixture point lies on the straight line FS and on a tie line, never on the binodal curve itself unless the mixture is just saturated.
K and β are different: K = 1.54 here says how much solvent is needed, β = 29.4 says how cleanly A is separated from B. A solvent with large K and β near 1 is useless.
In the lever rule E/M = RM/RE, the arm opposite E is RM. Swapping the arms gives E = 72.7 kg instead of 147.3 kg.
The plait point is where the layers become identical, not the richest possible extract.

quiz.a: The extract is the solvent-rich layer leaving a stage, carrying the transferred solute. The raffinate is the carrier-rich layer left after the solute has been partly removed.

quiz.q: A mixture whose point lies outside the binodal curve is stirred and left to settle. Why does it not form two layers?
quiz.a: Outside the curve the whole mixture is one stable liquid phase at that temperature. Two layers form only when the overall point lies inside the curve, where it sits on a tie line joining two equilibrium compositions; the lever rule then gives the amount of each layer.

quiz.q: List four properties of a good extraction solvent and give the reason for each.
quiz.a: High selectivity, so the extract is not diluted with carrier; high K, so less solvent is needed; low solubility in the carrier, so less solvent is lost; easy recovery (boiling point far from the solute, no azeotrope), so it can be recycled cheaply. Also a good density difference for quick settling.

quiz.q: A raffinate holds x<sub>A</sub> = 0.08, x<sub>B</sub> = 0.90 and the extract in equilibrium holds y<sub>A</sub> = 0.20, y<sub>B</sub> = 0.05. Find K and β.
50 kg of feed (40 % A in B) is mixed with 75 kg of pure S. Find the mass fractions at the mixture point and the ratio FM/MS.
quiz.a: M = 125 kg with 20 kg A, 30 kg B and 75 kg S: x<sub>A</sub> = 0.16, x<sub>B</sub> = 0.24, x<sub>S</sub> = 0.60. FM/MS = S/F = 75/50 = 1.5.

quiz.q: Two solvents give the same K for the solute. Solvent P dissolves 2 % of the carrier, solvent Q dissolves 12 %. Which do you choose, and what goes wrong with the other?
quiz.a: Choose P. With Q the extract carries much more carrier, so β is lower and the recovered solute is impure; more carrier must be separated from the solvent, and more Q is lost in the raffinate, raising make-up cost. Equal K means equal solvent flow, so the decision rests on mutual solubility, recovery cost and density difference.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plants recover acetic acid from dilute aqueous streams, purify penicillin with butyl acetate at controlled pH, refine copper with chelating extractants and reprocess nuclear fuel with tributyl phosphate. Instead of measuring every tie line, designers fit activity-coefficient models such as NRTL or UNIQUAC to a few data points and let a simulator draw the binodal curve. Pharmaceutical companies publish solvent-selection guides that rank solvents by safety, health and environmental impact. Search for liquid–liquid equilibrium data, NRTL model and solvent selection guide.
